title: Five remembrances
hook: I will age, sicken, die, be parted from what I love, and I am heir to my deeds

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old couple, and four things shared so they could stay side by side. Did you do one good thing side by side with someone? Today closes a week, with five lines to say to yourself. Day six hundred sixty-five.

Look back at this week. The gold-washer, refining slowly. Salt lost in the river. The three intoxications: youth, health and life. Dona, and remember me as awake. The firebrand. And the old couple, together. Now, four days ago, those three intoxications came with a quiet warning: the pride of being young, of being well, of being alive makes people careless. Today's sutta is the medicine for that pride. It's short enough to fit on a card. The Buddha says these five things should be reflected on often, by everyone: man or woman, householder or monk. Today: five remembrances.
screen: `A WEEK OF NUMBERED SAYINGS.` → `THE THREE INTOXICATIONS.` → `THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Here are the five, in plain words. One: I am of the nature to age; I haven't gone beyond aging. Two: I am of the nature to get sick; I haven't gone beyond sickness. Three: I am of the nature to die; I haven't gone beyond death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. Five: I am the owner of my deeds, heir to my deeds, born of my deeds, bound to my deeds; whatever I do, good or bad, I will inherit it. This sounds grim. But the sutta explains why each line helps. Thinking on aging, it says, wears down the pride of youth. Thinking on sickness wears down the pride of health. Thinking on death wears down the pride of being alive. Thinking on parting wears down the clinging to what's dear. And thinking on deeds wears down misconduct in body, speech and mind. The first four are about what you can't control. The fifth is about the one thing you can. That's the turn. You can't stop the clock or keep everyone forever. But what you do today becomes what you inherit. Heir is the key word: like an estate, your deeds are passed down to you, the good with the bad. In some monasteries and homes, these five are chanted as a daily reflection.
screen: `AGING, SICKNESS, DEATH.` · `PARTED FROM WHAT I LOVE.` · `EACH ONE WEARS DOWN A PRIDE.` · then, large: `HEIR TO MY DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Then, slowly, one line per few breaths, say them inwardly. I will grow old. I may grow ill. I will die. What I love will change, and I will part from it. I am heir to my deeds. If a line feels heavy, stay with the breath until it softens. Then let the last line point somewhere: what you do is yours to shape. The bell holds the time.
Five remembrances. Aging, sickness, death, parting, and deeds: the five things the Buddha asked everyone to reflect on often, to wear down pride and steady the hand. Today's word.
Your line: heir to my deeds. Today, before one choice, small or large, ask: is this something I'd like to inherit? Day six hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist monasteries and lay groups recite the five remembrances as part of morning or evening chanting, and teachers offer them as a reflection for anyone, ordained or not.

pairs: wears down the pride of youth
wears down the pride of health
wears down the pride of life

myth: the five remembrances are only for monks and nuns
the sutta says they're for everyone: women and men, householders and monastics.
the fifth remembrance is about deeds, not death
I am the owner and heir of my deeds.
the sutta says thinking on death makes people more careless
it says the opposite: it wears down the pride of being alive.

fork.setup: four of the five remembrances name things you can't change. what does the fifth name?
options: your deeds, which you will inherit.
fork.reveal: the fifth turns the list around: you can't stop aging or loss, but your deeds are yours, and you're their heir.

original.note: Pali kammadayada: 'heir of kamma,' from kamma, deed, and dayada, heir.

trapdoor: what you thought: the five remembrances are a gloomy list about death.
what it means: each line is a medicine for a particular pride, and the last gives you something to do.
what a scholar hears: the three prides of AN 3.38, youth, health and life, return here in AN 5.57 with their cure.

notes: AN 5.57 paraphrased. Confirm the full deeds formula (owner, heir, born of, bound to/related to, have as refuge) and that the script's shorter version is fair.
Confirm that the sutta pairs each reflection with the pride/clinging it wears down as given.
'Many Buddhists … still recite these five, often daily' is a general characterization; confirm it's fair across traditions.

Review (y2 editor pass): softened 'many Buddhists... often daily' in the teach and HOW (claims rule), cut 'the sutta knows it', and the practice no longer tells the listener the last line will feel like relief. Varied the 'Here's the practice' opener.
